objectives.text: Buy security at the lowest domestic price inside NATO and the EU: after being the alliance's laggard (a 2025 parliamentary vote on spending, then Golob's threat of a NATO-membership referendum), Janša's government has committed to reach 2% of GDP in 2026 and the NATO path of 3.5% core defence by 2035.

objectives.text: Keep the Croatian frontier quiet while keeping the legal win: Slovenia treats the 2017 Piran Bay arbitration award as binding, Croatia calls the process null; the two governments park the issue and cooperate on practical matters (border bridges agreement, 23 Jun 2025) because Zagreb is a co-member of the EU, the euro area, Schengen and NATO and the co-owner of Krško.

objectives.text: Secure low-carbon baseload from the one nuclear plant it has, shared with Croatia: a second unit (JEK2, estimated EUR 9.3-15.4bn) was to go to a consultative referendum on 24 Nov 2024, which parliament cancelled on 24 Oct 2024 (60-1-1); the project is alive but without a public mandate.

means.text: Open-economy integration with its neighbours rather than leverage over them: Germany (13.5% of goods exports in 2023), Italy (8.6%), Croatia (7.8%) and Austria (5.7%), plus a very large and unusual flow to Switzerland (27.3%); EU members take 55.5% of exports.

constraints.text: Parliamentary arithmetic. The 22 Mar 2026 election was inconclusive (Svoboda 29 seats, SDS 28 of 90, no bloc at 46); Janša was elected on 22 May 2026 by 51-36 with a 43-seat coalition (SDS, NSi, Democrats, SLS, Focus) plus the support of Resni.ca, so every foreign-policy reversal rests on a thin and untested majority.

constraints.text: A weak military and a divided public on NATO: the last ally to reach 2% (not before 2026), a junior-coalition party (Levica) that wants out of NATO and a poll cited at about 52% support for membership in 2025, down from 66% in 2003.

constraints.text: Croatia holds the other half of its infrastructure and its only sea access: Krško is owned jointly with Croatia's HEP, the Piran Bay award is unimplemented and the Slovenian government cannot enforce it without costing goodwill it needs on Schengen, the euro and the plant.

paradoxes.text: A foreign-policy identity that does not outlast the election. Golob's government spent the UN seat, the 2024 recognition of Palestine and the 2025 entry bans and arms embargo on Israel to make Slovenia a principled voice; within six months of the seat's end Janša's government let the embargo lapse, lifted the bans and took the Palestinian flag off the government building, so the capital built on the seat is partly spent and Slovenian policy reads as a pendulum rather than a line.

paradoxes.text: Betting on a patron who fell. Janša, a close ally of Viktor Orbán (whose circle financed Slovenian right-wing media, per RSF), returned to office a month after Orbán lost the April 2026 Hungarian election to Péter Magyar; the Hungarian axis that was to shield Ljubljana in the EPP and the Council is gone, and the Israel line now costs him a hearing in Berlin.

paradoxes.text: A legal victory that cannot be cashed. The 2017 arbitration gave Slovenia most of Piran Bay and a junction to the high seas; because Croatia walked out of the process in 2015 and refuses the award, pressing the claim would cost the Croatian cooperation on which Krško, the border bridges and Schengen depend, so the award is kept as a moral asset and parked.

grand_strategy.reading:
Slovenia is a small, rich, open economy whose strategy is to stay inside every
club (EU, euro, Schengen, NATO) and to spend as little as possible on anything
that is not membership. Its distinctive feature in 2022-26 is that the content
of foreign policy swings with the government while the anchors do not move:
Golob's Slovenia used the Security Council seat to be the EU's most outspoken
critic of Israel; Janša's Slovenia, since June 2026, pays its dues to NATO,
courts Trump and reopens to Israel. One signal that is not a row: Israel's
announced embassy in Ljubljana, the visible reward for the reversal.
What this card could not source and leaves open: Ukraine aid, Western Balkans
advocacy, China, Italy, Trieste and Koper, tariffs and the Hungarian media loan.

stances.note: Mirrors Croatia's own reading (HRV toward SVN: ally, stable, affinity) with the same sources, and adds Ljubljana's side. NATO and EU co-members (Art. 5, Art. 42(7)) and neighbours trading EUR 5.4bn a year, but Slovenia treats the 2017 Piran Bay award as binding while Croatia has rejected it since 2015: that open legal wound is why Slovenia's grade is 'reluctant' where Zagreb's is plain 'ally'. The two governments park it (2023 agreement to keep it out of daily politics; border-bridges agreement signed 23 Jun 2025 by Golob and Plenkovic) and co-own the Krsko plant. No source uses the phrase 'reluctant ally': the grade is our reading of the structure. Bond - grievance: the unimplemented award. Janša's government (from June 2026) has made no found statement on the border.

stances.note: NATO and EU co-member. Janša has been Orbán's closest partner in the EU (Orbán endorsed him on Slovenian TV in 2018 and Hungarian business circles bought into Slovenian right-wing media, per RSF; the Hungarian stake in Nova24TV was reported sold in 2022), which is the affinity. Orbán lost the April 2026 election to Péter Magyar, so the personal channel that defined the bond is gone; no Janša-Magyar statement was found, hence 'stable' and confidence C. Under Golob (2022-26) the two governments were distant, so 'ally' here is the co-membership floor plus the Janša affinity, not a Slovenia-wide alignment. The Hungarian loan referred to in the brief was not found in any source reached.

stances.note: Reversed in 2026. Under Golob (2025) Slovenia banned Ben-Gvir and Smotrich from entry, imposed an arms embargo and banned settlement imports - at that point a 'rival'. On 11 Jun 2026 Janša's government lifted the bans on Netanyahu and the two ministers, let the embargo lapse and lifted the settlement-import ban, 'to restore the conditions for a normal political dialogue'; Israel announced an embassy in Ljubljana. Janša strongly supports Israel and criticised the 2024 recognition of Palestine. Partner, not ally: no alignment, an EU member whose public and partners (Berlin) are critical of the line. Bond - affinity: the Janša government's sympathy, not a Slovenian national consensus (Mladina asks who supports his foreign policy).

The recognition itself is not reversed in any source found.

stances.note: Not adversary: no declared aim against Russia's existence or regime. Slovenia is an EU and NATO member under the EU sanctions regime, and a Russian intelligence network was found on its soil: two Russian 'illegals' posing as Argentine citizens were arrested in December 2022 and sentenced in July 2024 before leaving in the 1 Aug 2024 prisoner swap; one reported target was the EU energy regulator ACER in Ljubljana. Further 2022-26 spy cases were not found. No source uses the word 'rival': the grade is our reading (confidence C). Slovenia's gas and oil exposure to Russia was not sourced.

stances.note: NATO treaty ally (Art. 5), the structure; warming since June 2026 because Prime Minister Janša, a declared admirer of Trump, met Melania Trump's father Viktor Knavs at the US 250th-anniversary event in Ljubljana, attended the Trumps' UNGA reception and, by his account, invited Trump to Slovenia and was promised a visit (the promise is Janša's report, not independently confirmed). Under Golob the line was cool on Washington's Gaza policy at the Security Council. No source on tariffs or trade with the US was found. Bond - affinity: Janša's personal and ideological tie plus the Knavs family link, not a Slovenian consensus.

stances.note: Treaty member whose spending lagged: in July 2025 parliament voted (46-42, on a resolution by the Levica party) for a consultative referendum on raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, Golob answered by threatening a NATO-membership referendum and the vote was cancelled on 18 Jul 2025. Janša's government (June 2026) says Slovenia will reach 2% this year in the revised budget and follow the 3.5% core-defence path agreed for 2035; he said Slovenia is not doing it because NATO requires it. Reluctant because the friction is domestic and visible (Levica wants out, support for membership polled at about 52%); warming because the new government reverses the Golob-era stance. No source uses 'reluctant ally'; the grade is our reading from Defense News and the government's own statements.

relations_from.summary: Slovenia treats the 2017 Piran Bay arbitration award (most of the bay and a junction to the high seas) as binding; Croatia withdrew from the process in 2015 and does not implement it. In 2023 the two prime ministers agreed to keep the dispute out of daily politics. Mirrors Croatia's row toward Slovenia with the same sources.

the proceedings were contaminated and the award null; the Sabor rejected it entirely (Plenkovic, July 2023)

sources.title: Slovenia gets bulk of Piran Bay, 'junction' access to high seas
Traditionally good and friendly relations between Croatia and Slovenia, the border dispute takes time to resolve

relations_from.summary: Slovenia sold Croatia EUR 5.4bn of goods in 2025 (12.0% of Croatian imports) and bought EUR 3.0bn from it. Mirrors Croatia's trade row; the Slovenian-side figure for 2025 (Comtrade, US$5.46bn, up from US$5.10bn in 2024) agrees.
relations_from.note: Croatian customs-statistics figure (DZS table, EUR 5,409m); Slovenia's own statistics office release was not reached. Croatia was about 7.8% of Slovenian goods exports in 2023 (Statistics Slovenia via ACCIÓ).

relations_from.summary: The Krsko nuclear plant is owned jointly by Slovenia's GEN Energija and Croatia's HEP; a second unit (JEK2, EUR 9.3-15.4bn estimated) was to go to a consultative referendum on 24 Nov 2024, which the National Assembly cancelled on 24 Oct 2024 (60 for, 1 against, 1 abstention) citing a lack of public information on the project.
relations_from.note: The cited article says the plant is 'jointly owned' by HEP and GEN Energija; the 50/50 split is the standard description of the plant's ownership but is not stated in that article. The share of Slovenian electricity from Krsko was not sourced.

sources.title: Slovenia cancels referendum on Krsko nuclear power plant expansion

relations_from.summary: Germany took 13.5% of Slovenian goods exports in 2023, the largest EU destination; on Comtrade 2025 data it was US$8.2bn, about 10% of a total inflated by Swiss flows.
relations_from.note: SURS-based 2023 shares as reported by ACCIÓ; the Comtrade 2025 series (via Trading Economics) is not Slovenia's statistics office and is used only as a cross-check of ranking.

relations_from.note: An unusually large flow for a country of its size; the composition behind it (re-exports, pharmaceutical or gold trade) was not checked and no inference is drawn.

relations_from.summary: In July 2025 Golob's government banned Israel's National Security Minister Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Smotrich from entering Slovenia for inciting violence (17 Jul 2025, the first such measure by an EU member, per Fajon), then announced a full arms embargo (exports, imports and transit, with an exception for Slovenia's own security) and a ban on imports from settlements; Netanyahu was also barred in some reports. Lifted by Janša's government on 11 Jun 2026.

sources.title: Slovenia imposes arms embargo on Israel
Slovenia lifts entry ban on Israeli PM, arms embargo

relations_from.summary: On 11 Jun 2026 the new government lifted the entry bans on Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, let the arms embargo expire (calling it unnecessary given national law and EU export criteria) and ended the settlement-import ban, to 'restore the conditions for a normal political dialogue'; it also removed the Palestinian flag from the government building. Israel announced an embassy in Ljubljana the week before.

sources.title: Slovenia lifts entry ban on Israeli PM, arms embargo
Slovenia: Foreign policy, media control backlash (press digest of Delo, Mladina, Dnevnik)

relations_from.summary: On 4 Jul 2025 parliament voted 46-42 for a Levica resolution to hold a consultative referendum on raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030; Golob answered that the choice was to pay NATO dues or leave and announced a NATO-membership referendum; the National Assembly cancelled the spending referendum on 18 Jul 2025.

sources.title: Slovenia scraps defense-spending vote, seeks new kit with eye on NATO
Slovenia: NATO membership suddenly up for a vote

relations_from.summary: After the July 2026 Ankara summit (5% of GDP by 2035, of which 3.5% core defence) Prime Minister Janša committed Slovenia to reach 2% of GDP in 2026 through a revised budget and to follow the 2035 targets; on 14 Sep 2026 he said Slovenia strengthens its defence for its own security, not because NATO requires it.

sources.title: Prime Minister Janez Janša: We are strengthening our defence capabilities to ensure Slovenia's security

relations_from.summary: In June 2026 Janša met Viktor Knavs, Melania Trump's father, at the US 250th-anniversary event in Ljubljana; in September he attended the Trumps' reception for delegation heads at the UN General Assembly in New York and says he invited Trump to Slovenia, who promised to come (Janša's account).

relations_from.summary: Two Russian illegals posing as Argentine citizens, arrested in Ljubljana in December 2022, pleaded guilty in a closed trial to espionage and fake documents and were sentenced on 30-31 Jul 2024 to 19 months (time served); banned for five years, they were flown to Moscow in the 1 Aug 2024 prisoner swap. One reported target was the EU energy regulator ACER, based in Ljubljana.

relations_from.summary: Elected member of the UN Security Council in 2024-25 with presidencies in September 2024 and December 2025; it tabled five draft resolutions, four on Gaza, of which only Resolution 2728 (March 2024) was adopted; voted for Palestine's full UN membership in April 2024 and was one of 77 co-sponsors of the General Assembly resolution that passed 143-9-25.
